newsitem.title: SPAIN: Second Basque politician faces ETA death threat.
newsitem.headline: Second Basque politician faces ETA death threat.

text.p: With Spaniards still voicing outrage at the murder of a young politician by Basque separatist guerrillas, rebels have issued a threat to kill another of town councillor in the northern region.

An outcry at the assassination of Miguel Angel Blanco -- which brought millions of Spaniards on the streets to protest -- apparently did not deter rebels of the ETA group who threatened to kill Jose Luis Caso, a 63-year-old Basque politician from the ruling Popular Party (PP).

While the Basque town of Ermua buried councillor Blanco, 29, on Monday, rebels sprayed "You will be next" on a wall outside the home of his fellow PP politician in nearby Renteria, a government official said.
Analysts said ETA may be signalling that it plans to target low-ranking PP politicians generally.

"Caso will be unreachable and will probably go into hiding for now and ETA will go for someone else vulnerable in the Popular Party, someone not senior but who is close to state institutions, maybe in Madrid," said one analyst.

The government has vowed to smash the guerrilla group. Blanco's killing was the 10th ETA assassination this year. The group has killed more than 800 people in a 29-year fight for an independent state.

"Millions of Spaniards have not gone out onto the streets so that everything continues as before; everything is not going to continue as before," Angel Acebes, general coordinator of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's party, said.

Acebes, speaking after a special meeting of the party's executive with Aznar, said the Popular Party would join forces with all other political parties to implement specific measures to bolster the fight against ETA after the killing.

More than two million Spaniards took to the streets across the country on Monday to condemn the killing of Blanco who was kidnapped and then shot twice in the head after the government refused to transfer ETA inmates to Basque prisons.

On Tuesday, hundreds of thousands more mounted protests in several cities. In the southern city of Seville almost half a million demonstators packed the streets chanting "Basques yes, ETA no" and "Ermua, friend, Seville is with you".
Analysts said the government is now in a strong position but under pressure to calm anger in the country, although cautioning that any reaction should be balanced.
"If they go too far they risk an even greater violent backlash from ETA, but if they don't go far enough, Spaniards could take the law into their own hands," said one analyst.
In some areas that is exactly what ETA opponents have done.

In a number of Basque towns, demonstrators threw eggs and rocks at buildings used by ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna. In other areas, people painted signs on the doors of shops and bars run by ETA sympathisers, urging citizens to use other establishments.
The furious reaction to Blanco's killing, even among some ETA inmates and members of the group's political wing Herri Batasuna, may signal that the group is becoming more divided than ever.
"We may soon see a split between ETA and HB hardliners and the softliners, but this will not mean an end to violence," said one analyst.
ETA, which was formed in 1959 under the dictatorship of Francisco Franco to fight for a Basque state, split in the early 70s into a hardcore faction and a less violent wing.
